issues.legal_issue: An executing court cannot entertain an objection that a decree was passed without territorial jurisdiction.
material_facts: A partition decree was passed by a trial court and was later brought before that court for execution.
The judgment-debtor objected under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the decree was invalid because the trial court lacked territorial jurisdiction.
The executing court declined to consider the objection, but the High Court directed it to do so.
issues.conclusion: The objection to territorial jurisdiction could not be decided in execution, and the executing court was required to execute the decree as it stood.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires an objection to the place of suing to be raised at the earliest opportunity in the court of first instance and permits it to be entertained by an appellate or revisional court only if there has been a consequent failure of justice. Territorial jurisdiction is distinct from inherent jurisdiction over the subject matter. Under Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, an executing court cannot go behind a decree; an objection that requires investigation of facts cannot be raised in execution, and territorial-jurisdiction objections are not an exception to that rule. Kiran Singh v Chaman Paswan, Hiralal v Kalinath, Harshad Chiman Lal Modi v DLF Universal Ltd., Hasham Abbas Sayyad v Usman Abbas Sayyad, and Mantoo Sarkar v Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. support the distinction between territorial jurisdiction and jurisdiction over the subject matter.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The court is dealing with proceedings to execute an existing decree.
predicates.objection_based_on_territorial_jurisdict: A party objects that the court which passed the decree lacked territorial authority to hear the suit.

issues.definition: When a territorial-jurisdiction objection is raised in execution proceedings, the executing court must execute the decree without deciding that objection.

issues.legal_issue: An executing court cannot decide an objection to a decree that requires determination of the merits of the underlying dispute.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor argued that property relied on to establish the trial court's territorial jurisdiction did not belong to the common ancestor.
Deciding that contention would require consideration of the merits of the property dispute.
A first appeal challenging the decree, in which jurisdiction had also been raised, was pending.
issues.conclusion: The property-related contention was a matter of merits and, if pursued, had to be raised in the first appeal rather than decided by the executing court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, an executing court must take the decree according to its tenor and cannot go behind it; an objection requiring investigation of facts cannot be decided in execution. The Court stated that the property contention was a matter of merits for the appropriate court in the first appeal.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The court is dealing with proceedings to execute an existing decree.
predicates.objection_requires_determination_of_unde: Resolving the objection requires deciding a disputed matter that formed part of the merits of the underlying case.

issues.definition: When an objection in execution requires determination of the underlying merits, the executing court must not decide that objection.

issues.legal_issue: A remand order warrants appellate interference when it directs an executing court to decide an objection that is not maintainable in execution.
material_facts: The High Court set aside the executing court's refusal to consider the territorial-jurisdiction objection and remitted the matter for the executing court to decide it.
The remand therefore required the executing court to entertain an objection that it could not decide in execution.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, holding that the High Court had acted in excess of its jurisdiction; the order's remand character did not prevent interference.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the High Court had acted in excess of jurisdiction by directing the executing court to entertain an objection that did not lie in execution. It rejected the contention that the order was merely interlocutory and therefore did not warrant interference under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.

predicates.challenge_to_remand_order: A party challenges an order remitting a matter to a lower court for further proceedings.
predicates.remand_directs_decision_of_objection_not: The remand directs an executing court to decide an objection that it has no authority to determine in execution.

issues.definition: When a challenged remand directs an executing court to decide an objection it cannot determine in execution, appellate interference with the remand is warranted.
